A traumatic brain injury can flip life upside down without warning. One moment everything feels normal, and the next, medical appointments stack up, symptoms refuse to fade, and even simple decisions start to feel overwhelming. After a serious accident, many in Colorado wonder how a
head injury claim
actually works and whether legal action can help protect financial stability while recovery remains uncertain. At
Dormer Harpring
, we work with those whose brain injuries affect memory, focus, emotional balance, and long-term independence, guiding each step with clarity, intention, and steady advocacy from the start.
What is a Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI)?

A traumatic brain injury happens when an external force disrupts how the brain normally functions, often after a violent blow or sudden jolt to the head or body. In more difficult situations, an object may break through the skull and directly damage brain tissue. According to
Johns Hopkins Medicine
, TBI is a broad medical term that includes focal injuries affecting a specific area of the brain and diffuse injuries impacting multiple regions at once. Severity can range from a mild
concussion
to a life-altering injury that leads to a permanent disability or coma, which explains why symptoms and recovery timelines vary so widely.
Different Types of Damages in Head Injury Cases

Brain injuries rarely stay confined to one area of life. Colorado law recognizes this reality and allows compensation that reflects the full scope of harm. In most cases, damages fall into two primary categories, each playing an important role in a well-supported claim.
Economic damages address the financial strain caused by a brain injury and often include:
Emergency medical care, diagnostic testing, and ongoing neurological treatment
Rehabilitation services, therapy, and assistive devices
Lost income and reduced earning capacity when returning to work becomes difficult or impossible
Non-economic damages focus on the personal impact of living with a brain injury, which may involve:
Chronic pain, headaches, and ongoing fatigue
Cognitive challenges such as memory loss or difficulty concentrating
Emotional distress, mood changes, and loss of enjoyment in daily activities
In a properly developed
head injury claim
, these non-economic losses often carry significant weight because they shape long-term independence rather than short-term inconvenience.

children.text: What are TBI’s Common Causes?

Traumatic brain injuries happen across Colorado in many everyday situations, especially when safety failures collide with high-risk environments. Falls remain the leading cause statewide, particularly among older adults and young children, and often trace back to unsafe property conditions, poor maintenance, or inadequate supervision. Vehicle-related accidents also account for a large number of brain injuries, including crashes involving cars, motorcycles, bicycles, and pedestrians on city streets and mountain highways.

Colorado’s outdoor culture adds another layer of risk. High-impact sports and recreational activities such as skiing, snowboarding, mountain biking, and contact athletics lead to many TBIs each year. Assaults and acts of violence, including domestic violence and gunshot wounds, also contribute to serious brain injuries. As explained by the
Mayo Clinic
, traumatic brain injury commonly results from violent blows or jolts to the head or body, or from objects penetrating brain tissue.
Understanding Traumatic Brain Injury Claims

A traumatic brain injury claim focuses on accountability when another party’s negligence causes harm. Under Colorado law, compensation may be available when unsafe property conditions, distracted driving, defective products, or inadequate security lead to brain trauma. These cases often prove more challenging than other injury claims because symptoms may take time to appear, and imaging does not always reveal the full extent of neurological damage right away.

A strong claim weaves together medical records, expert insight, and real-world consequences to show how the injury changed daily life, employment prospects, and future needs, creating leverage during negotiations.
How to Prove a Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI) in Court?
Proving a traumatic brain injury requires telling a clear, credible story supported by evidence showing how the injury occurred and how it affects daily life.
Step 1: Seek Medical Attention

Getting medical care right away protects both health and legal rights. Emergency evaluations, neurological exams, imaging studies, and follow-up treatment records help connect the traumatic event to the symptoms that follow, strengthening any future brain injury lawsuit.
Step 2: Gather Evidence

Medical records matter, though they are rarely enough on their own. Accident reports, photographs, surveillance footage, witness statements, and employment documentation help explain how the injury happened and why everyday functioning changed afterward. Personal journals tracking headaches, memory problems, mood shifts, and fatigue often add valuable context to a
head injury claim
, helping decision-makers understand lived experience rather than relying only on test results.
Step 3: Consult with Our Personal Injury Lawyer

Legal guidance brings everything together. We evaluate liability, work with medical and financial professionals, and present claims in a format Colorado courts recognize as credible and thorough. We also handle communication with insurers so recovery can remain the priority.
How to Maximize the Damages You Get for a Brain Injury

Maximizing recovery takes preparation and consistency throughout the life of a claim. Following medical recommendations shows commitment to healing and reduces opportunities for insurers to question the seriousness of a brain injury. Careful documentation of ongoing symptoms and functional limitations helps demonstrate why compensation should address long-term care rather than short-term costs.

The way a case is presented also matters. Connecting medical findings to everyday consequences helps courts and insurers understand what ongoing care and financial stability will realistically require over time.
What Factors Influence a Head Injury Claim?
Several connected factors shape the value and outcome of a claim. When compensation and overall case strength are evaluated, the following factors usually carry the most weight:
Severity and permanence of the brain injury
Strength and consistency of medical documentation
Quality of evidence showing negligence or fault
Impact on employment, independence, and family life
Comparative fault considerations under Colorado law
Taken together, these elements explain why careful case development often determines whether a claim reaches a fair resolution.
Time Limit for Filing a Traumatic Brain Injury Claim
Timing matters in every traumatic brain injury claim. Even strong evidence and well-documented losses can lose value if deadlines pass. Colorado law sets strict statutes of limitations for
personal injury
cases, and missing these deadlines typically ends the right to
pursue compensation

Most negligence-based injury claims in Colorado must be filed within two years, while cases involving motor vehicle accidents usually allow three years. Because brain injury symptoms sometimes develop gradually, early legal evaluation helps preserve evidence, protect filing deadlines, and keep the claim viable.
